## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷadhammapālajātaka* (Ja 358), titled *The Shorter Tale of Dhammapāla* in English, is a canonical narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection. The frame narrative is set at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), where the Buddha related the tale concerning Devadatta's plots to kill the Bodhisatta. In the story, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the seven-month-old infant prince Dhammapāla [Ohnuma 2012; Fausböll 1883]. When the boy's mother, Queen Candā, is absorbed in playing with the child and fails to stand up to greet the king (Mahāpatāpa), the enraged monarch summons the executioner and commands him to lop off the infant's hands, feet, and head, and strip his flesh [Ohnuma 2012]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the cruel king is revealed to have been Devadatta, Queen Candā was Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, and Prince Dhammapāla was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1883].

In Theravāda exegetical and doctrinal literature, the narrative serves as a prominent meditation exemplar for subduing hatred (*paṭigha*) and anger toward hostile adversaries [Narasabho 1971; Ohnuma 2012]. The Bodhisatta's conduct during this life is cited by commentators to illustrate forbearance, equanimity, and the perfection of loving-kindness characterized by extending boundless welfare to all beings (*sabbasattesu anodhiso hitūpasaṃhāralakkhaṇāya mettāya*), maintaining complete benevolence even toward those intent on executing him [Endo 1997; Narasabho 1971; Ohnuma 2012].
